name: GRACILE syndrome
aliases: growth retardation, aminoaciduria, cholestasis, iron overload, lactic acidosis and early death
Finnish lactic acidosis with hepatic haemosiderosis

reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / Suchy Liver Disease in Children
clinicalPearls: A severe autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder caused by mutations in BCS1L, first described as a Finnish-heritage disease
The acronym captures the phenotype: growth restriction, aminoaciduria, cholestasis, iron overload, lactic acidosis, and early death
Presents in the neonatal period with profound, often fatal lactic acidosis and intrauterine growth restriction
Hepatic involvement includes cholestasis with iron accumulation (haemosiderosis) resembling neonatal haemochromatosis
Renal tubular dysfunction produces a generalised aminoaciduria
BCS1L encodes a chaperone required for assembly of complex III of the respiratory chain, so its deficiency impairs oxidative phosphorylation
Care is supportive and largely palliative; the Finnish founder (S78G) variant tends to cause the most severe, rapidly lethal form
reference.pathophysiology: GRACILE syndrome results from biallelic mutations in BCS1L, which encodes a chaperone essential for incorporating the Rieske iron-sulphur protein into complex III of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Impaired complex III assembly disrupts oxidative phosphorylation, causing severe lactic acidosis, and deranges cellular iron handling, leading to hepatic iron overload. The multisystem energy failure manifests as intrauterine growth restriction, cholestatic liver disease, renal tubulopathy with aminoaciduria, and typically death in infancy. The classic Finnish founder mutation produces an especially severe course.
additionalDifferentials: Other mitochondrial respiratory chain and DNA depletion disorders
Congenital lactic acidosis (pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, respiratory chain defects)
Renal Fanconi syndrome of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Liver function tests, serum bile acids, ferritin and iron studies
Urine amino acids demonstrating generalised aminoaciduria
Liver biopsy showing cholestasis and iron deposition
Respiratory chain enzyme analysis (reduced complex III activity)
redFlags: Rapidly progressive liver failure with coagulopathy
Marked hepatic iron overload mimicking neonatal haemochromatosis
Multiorgan failure with growth restriction in early infancy
reference.prognosis: The classic Finnish form is usually fatal within days to a few months of birth; milder BCS1L phenotypes with longer survival exist, but overall prognosis is poor and management is largely supportive and palliative.
pitfalls: Mistaking the hepatic iron overload for isolated neonatal haemochromatosis and missing the mitochondrial basis
Failing to measure lactate in a sick, growth-restricted neonate
Overlooking renal tubular dysfunction as a diagnostic clue
Not offering genetic counselling given the autosomal recessive inheritance and founder effect
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
Suchy, Sokol & Balistreri, Liver Disease in Children
management: Recognise that no disease-modifying therapy corrects the BCS1L complex III defect, so care is supportive and directed at the multisystem energy failure
Manage the profound lactic acidosis with buffering and careful fluid and electrolyte support in a neonatal intensive care setting
Treat cholestatic liver disease with fat-soluble vitamin supplementation and ursodeoxycholic acid, alongside high-energy nutritional support for growth restriction
Correct the electrolyte, bicarbonate and amino acid losses of the renal tubulopathy
Avoid iron supplementation and monitor hepatic iron overload rather than adding to the iron burden
Involve palliative and comfort care early given the frequently fatal course, supporting the family throughout
Coordinate neonatology, hepatology and metabolic (mitochondrial) specialist input
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with carrier testing and prenatal or preimplantation options for the family
